text: It may be objected that the chapter merely follows the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports what its persons feel and never explains either their feelings or their motives; and the objection is perhaps in part just. Yet the reticence of this chapter is deliberate, and the narrator knows what he is doing. Restraint, in his voice, is a kind of accusation; for he can tell what his characters feel when he will, and elsewhere he does: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps.
